summary: Redwood AE + SE demoed Hosted API chat and text generation features focusing on streaming responses, request params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and retry/backoff behavior. Customer (Monarch Logistics) is interested in lower-latency inference for chat assistants in internal logistics tools, wants benchmarking and security docs. Agreed to pilot and share artifacts.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Jordan with Redwood Inference. we have priya from our SE team and then we'll jump into a quick hosted API demo — chat and text generation basics, streaming and retry patterns.
[00:10] Alex (CTO): Hi all, Alex here. quick context — Monarch builds a logistics ops chat for drivers and dispatch, latency's pretty important, we're currently using a managed endpoint but seeing variable p95s.
[00:22] Jordan: got it, thanks. priya will show the console and then a live request flow.
[00:35] Priya (SE): hey! i'll start with a quick architecture slide, then hands-on. Redwood Hosted API gives you text + chat endpoints, streaming, function calls, and we surface model-tier perf profiles.
[00:50] Mia (ML Eng): curious about streaming — do you do chunked SSE? webhooks?
[00:56] Priya: we support streaming via server-sent events and libraries have helpers for chunk assembly. demo in a sec.
[01:10] Jordan: high level — hosted is great for quick time-to-value, if you need reserved throughput look at dedicated, and private is for VPC/on-prem.
[01:25] Tom (PM): timeline wise — aiming for a pilot in 3 weeks, so need to know integration effort.
[01:32] Priya: integration is mostly an API key and standard REST calls, we'll share a sample repo. request params are familiar: model, temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, and also streaming flag.
[01:45] [02:00] Priya: ok switching to the console — here's the model catalog, you can see curated open models with measured latencies and token costs. note the perf profile on the right.
[02:15] Jordan: quick Q — what are your target latency numbers?
[02:20] Alex: p95 under 400ms ideally for short prompts (<=128 tokens).
[02:28] Priya: that's doable for many smaller models on our hosted tier, but we should benchmark with your noise and prefix length. caching and KV cache prefix can help — though sorry, my bad, i said KV cash earlier, it's KV cache.
[02:45] Mia: what about retries? we see occasional 5xx from our current vendor and our clients explode with duplicates.
[02:52] Priya: good question. recommended pattern: client-side idempotency keys for replays, exponential backoff with jitter. we also expose a request_id on each response so you can de-dupe server-side. will demo retry headers.
[03:10] [03:30] Priya: live coding — sending a streaming chat request. (typing noises) here's the curl and then the node example. note we set streaming=true and the API returns chunks with partial text + delta tokens.
[03:50] Jordan: you'll see how the UI reassembles the stream into a single response. also ability to cancel mid-stream if user navigates away.
[04:05] Tom: do you provide SDKs for JS and python?
[04:10] Jordan: yep, official SDKs. we also have examples for retries and backoff baked in.
[04:20] Priya: demo output — streaming comes through in ~120ms for first byte in this example, then continuous tokens.
[04:35] Mia: do you support partial function calling? like function args streamed?
[04:40] Priya: streaming function call support is experimental but yes we stream deltas for function call metadata and args. a few customers use it.
[04:55] [05:15] Alex: can you talk about tokenization mismatch / billing surprises? we had an issue where system prompts spiked tokens.
[05:22] Jordan: we show token breakdown in the console per request and a token-level cost view in Console/Optimize, so you can identify prompt tokens vs generated tokens and set hard maxes.
[05:40] Priya: also recommend prefix caching for stable system prompts; that's where KV cache helps reduce repeat cost.
[05:55] Tom: security — need SOC2 and KMS integration.
[06:00] Jordan: we support SOC 2 attestations, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; hosted has encryption at rest with provider-managed KMS but we can talk about enterprise options. I'll share security docs.
[06:20] Mia: data retention — do you keep request logs?
[06:23] Priya: default retention is 30 days for debug logs in hosted, but enterprise customers can extend or opt-out; audit logs and access controls available.
[06:35] [07:00] Priya: back to demo — parameter tuning. temperature affects randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling, lower top_p reduces rare tokens. max_tokens limits generation length. we usually recommend starting at temp=0.2 for deterministic suggestions and higher for creative tasks.
[07:30] Jordan: show canary & rollout options?
[07:35] Priya: yes — in Console you can do per-route model pinning and gradual rollout to a model variant, plus automatic fallback to cheaper/broader models if the target is degraded.
[07:50] Alex: streaming reliability — how do you handle mid-stream failures?
[07:54] Priya: if a chunk fails mid-stream we return an error event and the client should either retry with idempotency key or resume where possible. resume support depends on the model and KV cache state. we show a sequence_id in chunks to detect gaps.
[08:20] [08:45] Mia: curious about throughput — how many concurrent streams per key?
[08:48] Jordan: hosted has rate limits by tier, we can provide expected concurrency numbers; Dedicated gives reserved concurrency. we'll include rate limit table.
[09:00] Priya: quick demo of retry header — when we return 429 or 503 we include a recommended-retry-after and a request_id. recommended backoff pattern: base 200ms, exponential x2, jitter cap ~2s.
[09:25] Tom: about partial outputs causing duplicates — you mentioned de-dupe via request_id, is that returned for streaming first chunk as well?
[09:32] Priya: yes first chunk includes request_id, so if you retry you can compare. but for safety use client-side idempotency tokens on create calls.
[09:45] [10:15] Jordan: show sample integration — node snippet, python snippet, and the SDK's high-level chat helper.
[10:30] Mia: latency numbers in demo seem optimistic — are they measured in a US region? we're in EU primarily.
[10:36] Priya: demo was run in us-west; we have eu regions and latency will differ, we'll run benchmarks in eu-west for you.
[10:50] Alex: does streaming increase cost?
[10:53] Jordan: cost is per token regardless of streaming; streaming just changes delivery. you can also set max tokens to control cost.
[11:05] [11:30] Priya: edge cases — if you have long context windows we recommend quantized model variants or dedicated capacity, otherwise latency and token cost climb.
[11:45] Mia: can you pin a model version per route? we need predictable responses for compliance.
[11:50] Priya: yes per-route model pinning and rollout history with diffs in console.
[12:05] Tom: what about partial failures when a function call fails at the end of stream — does Redwood do automatic fallback?
[12:10] Priya: we can configure policy-level fallbacks to a different model or region automatically; fallback preserves idempotency keys where possible.
[12:30] [12:50] Jordan: quick note on observability — Console shows token-level cost, latency histograms, per-route traces, and error logs. you can export logs via S3 or SIEM connectors.
[13:05] Alex: do you have any customers in logistics space?
[13:10] Jordan: yes a few — reference call available, i'll connect you.
[13:20] Mia: for the pilot we'll need to run a throughput test with our typical prompt mix and prefix-blowup scenarios.
[13:26] Priya: perfect — share the prompt set and expected QPS, we'll set up a benchmark job.
[13:40] [14:00] Priya: now showing a failure/retry simulation. i'm forcing a 503 on the second chunk, the client receives an error event and we show recommended retry policy.
[14:15] Tom: does the SDK handle exponential backoff automatically?
[14:20] Priya: the SDK has an opt-in retry helper with idempotency token generation, but we leave it configurable.
[14:30] Jordan: cost control features in Optimize — batching, prefix cache suggestions, and quantization recommendations per workload.
[14:45] Mia: curious about batching with streaming — do they conflict?
[14:50] Priya: batching is at serving layer; streaming can still work but first-byte latency may be affected if a batch waits. Optimize recommends batch sizes per SLO.
[15:05] [15:30] Alex: are there SLA numbers for hosted?
[15:35] Jordan: hosted has best-effort SLAs; Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency tiers. for enterprise requirements we usually move customers to Dedicated or Private.
[15:50] Mia: what's the onboarding friction for Private?
[15:53] Priya: Private is heavier — VPC peering, customer-managed KMS, and optional on-prem agent; onboarding usually 4-8 weeks depending on network approvals.
[16:10] [16:40] Priya: demo wrap — sample curl for streaming, node snippet, python snippet, and retry pattern shown.
[16:55] Tom: any gotchas with SDKs and browsers?
[17:00] Jordan: we recommend server-side proxy for API keys; browser use requires tokenization and limited scopes.
[17:15] Mia: can we restrict models or disable certain capabilities per team?
[17:18] Priya: yes role-based controls and per-route policy restrictions.
[17:30] [18:00] Alex: ok next steps — pricing, security docs, and a pilot.
[18:05] Jordan: i'll send pricing tiers, priya will send code samples and retry guidance. we'll run a eu-region benchmark once we have your prompt set.
[18:20] Tom: timeline check — we'll aim to confirm stakeholders by next tuesday.
[18:30] Priya: anything else on streaming or params?
[18:35] Mia: maybe one more — how do you surface tokenization differences across models?
[18:40] Priya: we include tokenizer preview in Console and token-count on each request example.
[19:00] [19:30] Jordan: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and the pilot plan.
[19:40] Alex: thanks, good session.
[19:45] (call audio drops briefly, small crosstalk)
[20:00] --- End of recorded meeting transcript (partial) ---

Notes: transcript above contains timestamps up to ~20 minutes in this export; actual meeting duration 38 minutes — remainder included Q&A and internal alignment. some transcription glitches present (KV cash -> KV cache, small misattribution).
